ch01.note: The idiom is 投石问路, literally to toss a stone to ask the road: a tentative probe thrown out ahead to see how the ground lies before one commits. The Reuters interview was the Juntong's stone.

ch01.anchor: Gu Shenyan poured him a glass of brandy
ch01.note: Gu Shenyan's given name, 慎言 (shèn yán), means “guarded in speech, watch your words” — a fitting name for a spymaster, and one the story quietly turns on. Chinese personal names carry plain lexical sense, and several in this book are chosen to tell.
The Red House (红房子) was a celebrated French restaurant in the Shanghai concessions and a fashionable place to be seen — cover enough, in itself, for two strangers to share a table before a killing.

ch02.note: The idiom is 鱼龙混杂, “fish and dragons jumbled together”: a place where the worthy and the worthless, the honest broker and the cutthroat, mingle past telling one from another — the wartime concession exactly.

ch02.anchor: you within me, and me within you
ch02.note: A set phrase, 你中有我，我中有你, “in you there is me, in me there is you”: two services so riddled with each other's agents that they interpenetrate. Gu states the first law of the trade, and the novel proceeds to prove it on every side.

Zhu Yizhen's given name is 怡贞; Lin calls her by the doubled endearment 贞贞 (Zhenzhen). The 贞 means fidelity, constancy, a woman's chastity — a quiet irony to hang on a character who lives by divided loyalties, and between two men.

ch02.anchor: Ji Zhongyuan sat under the lamp
ch02.note: Ji Zhongyuan's given name, 中原 (Zhōngyuán), is the Central Plain, the ancient heartland of China — a resonant thing for a Communist agent to be called, and, like “Old Ji,” almost certainly a nom de guerre rather than the name he was born with.

ch03.anchor: shrouded in horsehide on the field
ch03.note: “Shrouded in horsehide” renders 马革裹尸, from the Eastern Han general Ma Yuan, who vowed to die on the frontier and be carried home wrapped in a horse's hide rather than end in bed: the classic image of an honorable death in the field. Old Pan answers a real question with a slogan.

ch03.anchor: the dark spot under the lamp
ch03.note: The image is 灯下黑, “darkness beneath the lamp”: the ground directly under a lamp is the one place its light will not reach, so the safest hiding place is the one nearest the danger. Lin means the Japanese quarter, hidden under the occupier's own nose.
Tieguanyin (铁观音, “Iron Goddess of Mercy”), a prized oolong tea from Fujian.

ch05.anchor: A man who is never dissolute wastes his youth
ch05.note: A saying, 人不风流枉少年: to pass one's youth without ever being dashing or dissolute is to waste it. Gu, the aesthete, offers it only half in jest.

ch06.note: The word rendered “rebel” is 叛逆者 (pànnìzhě), the novel's title. It is not the same as 叛徒 (pàntú), “traitor,” the word used of the turncoat Ding Mocun: a 叛逆者 is one who rebels, turns, breaks faith — a wider and more searching term, and the book's true subject, for it is Lin Nansheng's own allegiance that the war will unmake and remake.

“Dyed red” (染红): red is the color of the Communists, and to be dyed red is to have been won over to their cause and steeped in it. Ten years in the movement, Gu means, have made Meng one of them in fact, not merely in cover.
A kabushiki-gaisha (株式会社) is a Japanese joint-stock company. Under the occupation such a firm was a natural front for an intelligence post.

ch07.note: The plum (梅) flowers in the last of the winter cold, before any other tree, and so stands in Chinese tradition for purity, endurance, and integrity kept under hardship. An “Ode to the Plum Blossom” run in a newspaper is at once an innocent cover and a loyalist's creed — the right poem to carry a call that must not look like one.
